François Coillard
frahn-SWAH kwah-YAR
proper noun
French; François, “Frenchman” or “free one,” and Coillard, a French surname. Borne by the Huguenot-descended Protestant missionary to the Barotse of the upper Zambezi (1834–1904).

📖 Biblical Definition

François Coillard, a Frenchman of Huguenot stock sent by the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society, gave his life first to the Basuto of southern Africa and then, in his later years, to the pioneering of a mission among the Barotse in the valley of the upper Zambezi, a region hard of access and long unreached by the gospel. With his devoted wife Christina at his side, he pressed into that far country, enduring the caprice of native kings, the ravages of fever, and the crushing loss of fellow labourers and of his beloved wife herself, yet he would not turn back from the door the LORD had opened. He translated and taught, planted the seed of the Word among a heathen people, and laid the foundations of a church in Barotseland at great and personal cost. His whole course was governed by a settled trust in the providence of God, and when hindered on every side he was wont to say that when God shuts one door He opens another. His life preaches that the pioneer’s path is a way of sacrifice and bereavement, that the gospel advances often through the graves of those who carry it, and that the servant who walks by faith may commit both his losses and his labours to a Father who does all things well. The blood and tears of the Coillards became, under God, the seed of a church among a people once wholly in darkness.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A Huguenot-descended missionary who pioneered the gospel among the Barotse of the Zambezi.

expand to see more

A Frenchman (1834–1904) of Huguenot descent, sent by the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society.

A labourer first among the Basuto, then a pioneer to the Barotse of the upper Zambezi.

A husband whose wife Christina shared his toils and whose loss he bore in the field.

A translator and teacher who planted a church in Barotseland at great personal cost.

A man of settled trust in providence, holding that when God shuts one door He opens another.

📖 Key Scripture

Rev 3:8 — "I know thy works: behold, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it: for thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name."

Joh 12:24 — "Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit."

Rom 8:28 — "And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose."

Heb 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers providence and sacrifice in pioneer missions.

expand to see more

Coillard’s name is preserved not because error has fastened upon it, but because his sacrifice and his unshaken confidence in providence rebuke an age that expects gospel advance without cost or bereavement. He buried his wife and fellow labourers, yet held to the open door.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from his life is that the pioneer’s path is one of sacrifice, and that except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die it abideth alone. His trust that all things work together for good to them that love God, and his confidence in the door no man can shut, recover for us the doctrine of providence, under which the servant may commit his griefs and his gains alike to a Father who does all things well.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

A Huguenot root nourished his faith; the deeper root was the wheat-corn dying to bring forth much fruit.

expand to see more

François — “Frenchman” or “free one,” of Huguenot lineage.

Coillard — a French surname carried into the African interior.

Rooted in Joh 12:24—the corn of wheat dying to bring forth much fruit.

Grounded in Rom 8:28, all things working together for good to them that love God.

A pilgrim who died in faith, seeing the promises afar off (Heb 11:13).
